/journal/one-city-two-verdicts.title: One city, forty-four monitors, two verdicts — Swechha
/journal/one-city-two-verdicts.description: For 125 of 286 hours, Delhi’s worst monitor was over the legal limit while the average of all forty-four was under it. Two honest summaries, two verdicts.

standfirst: For 125 of 286 hours, Delhi's worst monitor was above the legal limit while the average of every monitor reporting was below it. Both are honest summaries of the same instruments, and they disagree about whether the law was broken.

frame.alt: The Delhi skyline flattened into silhouette by smog

headings.matters: Why the choice of summary is the finding
headings.ours: What survives, and what this site chose

leads.happened: Swechha keeps every hourly reading CPCB publishes for Delhi, as first seen and with every later revision. This is what 286 consecutive hours of it contain.

happened: Between 21:00 on 25 August 2026 and 09:00 on 14 September 2026, this site recorded 286 hourly observations of Delhi's air. Each one covers the whole monitoring network: 45 distinct monitors appear across the window, with between 42 and 45 of them reporting in any given hour.

In 275 of those 286 hours, the worst-reading monitor in the city was above the Central Pollution Control Board's 24-hour limit of 100 on the index. In 150 of them, the unweighted mean of every monitor reporting was above it.

The two measures therefore disagreed in 125 hours — a little under half the window. In each of those hours one honest description of Delhi's air said the limit was broken and another honest description of the same instruments said it was not.
matters: Neither figure is wrong. A limit set for what a person breathes is broken the moment somebody is breathing air above it, and the worst monitor is the only summary that reports that. A limit read as a description of a city of twenty million is better served by an average, and the worst monitor is a poor description of anywhere but its own kerb.

The gap between them is not small and it is not stable. The median distance between the worst monitor and the mean across these 286 hours is 97 index points. The narrowest hour was 31 points apart; the widest was 313.

So the choice of summary is not a presentational one. It decides the verdict, and it decides it differently from hour to hour. Anybody quoting a single number for Delhi's air has made that choice, whether or not they said so.

data: The sharpest hour in the window was 16:00 on 3 September. Aya Nagar read 204 — Poor — while the mean across the network was 73, which is Satisfactory, and only three of the 44 monitors reporting were above the limit at all. One monitor in the south of the city was carrying almost the whole of that hour's breach.

The title of worst monitor does not circulate evenly. Fifteen stations held it at least once, which sounds like a city where the burden moves around. Two of them held it in more than two-thirds of all hours: Wazirpur in 121 and Anand Vihar in 75. Four stations were the worst exactly once each.

So both of the obvious readings are wrong. Delhi's pollution is not uniform, and it is not scattered either. It is concentrated in a small number of places that are almost always the worst, with a long tail of hours where somewhere else briefly takes the title.

The median hour had 25 of 44 monitors above the limit. That is the figure that sits between the two headline measures and is not reported by either: most of the network is usually over, which is why the mean spends half the window over too — and a quarter to a third of it is usually under, which is why the mean can sit below the limit while somebody's neighbourhood is at 204.
ours: The claim that survives every argument about method is the narrow one: for 125 hours out of 286, two defensible summaries of one set of instruments returned opposite answers to the question the limit exists to settle. That needs no model, no weighting scheme and no second source. It is a count over readings CPCB published.

It also changes what a reader should ask of any air figure. Not "is this number right" but "which of the two questions is it answering" — the one about the city, or the one about the worst place in it.

This site publishes the worst monitor, named. The reason is that a limit written for human lungs is broken where a person is standing rather than on average, and the station's name is printed beside the number so the choice is visible rather than assumed. The mean is kept in the record alongside it, which is how this piece could be written at all — and it is worth saying that the mean is what this site led with until August 2026, so the choice described here is one we have made both ways.
known: Across 286 consecutive hourly observations, the worst Delhi monitor exceeded the CPCB 24-hour limit of 100 in 275 hours.
The unweighted mean of all reporting monitors exceeded it in 150 of the same hours.
The two measures gave opposite verdicts in 125 hours.
Fifteen distinct stations were the city's worst at least once; Wazirpur and Anand Vihar accounted for 68.5% of all hours between them.
The median gap between the worst monitor and the mean was 97 index points.
uncertain: Whether this holds through the winter. The window is late monsoon into early September, which is one of Delhi's cleaner stretches. When the whole network is over the limit together, the two measures will agree far more often — and the interesting disagreement may be a feature of the shoulder season rather than of the year.

How the mean used here compares with CPCB's own published city figure. This one is unweighted; CPCB weights stations by population on a 2km grid. The two are not the same number and the difference is not estimated here.

Whether the concentration at Wazirpur and Anand Vihar is about emissions near those two monitors, about where the network happens to have been built, or about both. A monitor records where it is standing, and the map of monitors is not a map of the city.

What any of the index distances mean in concentration. The AQI is piecewise-linear, so a gap of 97 index points is not a gap of 97 of anything a person breathes, and it is not comparable across bands.
Whether the 11 hours in which even the worst monitor was under the limit share anything — rain, wind, hour of day. The window is too short to say.
watch: The same comparison run across a winter month, when the network is over the limit together. If the disagreement rate collapses, this is a shoulder-season finding; if it does not, it is a structural one.
Whether Wazirpur and Anand Vihar keep their share as the season turns, or whether the winter's worst monitors are somewhere else entirely.
Any city-level figure quoted in public without saying which of the two it is.
The monthly record pages, where the same observations are published hour by hour and can be counted again by anybody who disagrees with this.
